newsitem.title: USA: NYS voters call lack of a budget "serious" - poll.
newsitem.headline: NYS voters call lack of a budget "serious" - poll.

text.p: New York State voters said the state's lack of a budget was a serious problem, with most blaming both Gov George Pataki and the legislature for missing the April 1 deadline, a survey showed on Thursday.

"Does anyone care whether Albany adopts the state budget on time? To our surprise, we find that this is not just an issue for government insiders," said Maurice Carroll, director of Quinnipiac College Polling Institute, in prepared remarks.

While the Republican governor, who is considered a potential presidential challenger in 2000, kept about the same overall approval rating, his handling of the budget slipped into negative territory at 36 to 51 percent, in the institute's latest poll. This was down from a favorable 45 to 42 percent in a March survey.

Similarly, by a 39 to 52 percent margin, the 917 New Yorkers surveyed from April 14 to 20 disappoved of how Pataki, who has proposed big tax cuts in estate taxes plus an ambitious five-year plan to cut school property taxes, has handled taxes. The previous poll showed a near dead heat on the issue.
Still, Pataki got a 54 to 35 percent overall approval rating in the survey, which has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percent.
And the Republican governor, who has proposed tuition hikes for state universities, got a negative 40 to 48 percent rating on education.

Albany lawmakers, who last year set a national record for late budgets, might start to feel the heat for their failure to enact a pact on time this year. About 55 percent of the survey group called the lack of a budget a "very serious" problem, while 32 percent said it was somewhat serious. Only 13 percent disagreed.
